extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of 18th-century English literature; scholars researching Addison, Steele, and The Spectator
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and annotation of essayistic passages from The Spectator (Addison & Steele), extracting character-types, social customs, and authorial judgments for literary-historical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character of a Rake
rubrics_metrics.description: A Rake is a man always to be pitied; his faults proceed not from choice or inclination, but from strong passions and appetites in youth too violent for the curb of reason, good sense, good manners, and good nature. He sins and repents repeatedly and is miserable because he has remedy (reason) in his possession but does not use it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steele's account emphasizes pity rather than contempt: the rake's vices arise from excess of desirable qualities (imagination, compassion), not from studied wickedness. Examples and contrasts (e.g., Nobilis) are used to show that to be a rake one must be vicious against his will; imitators and second-hand vice are especially nauseous. Use this as a criterion when evaluating fictional or essayistic portrayals: is the rake portrayed as pitiable, driven by passion, and exhibiting cyclical remorse rather than deliberate malice?

rubrics_metrics.name: Coquette (female character)
rubrics_metrics.description: A coquette is a woman who lives in continual misapplication of her beauty: she practices affectations that disfigure her charms (e.g., the prettiest lisp), poring at people with half-shut eyes, and directs her regard toward the chief person present; she can giggle at divine service yet compose herself before a rich man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steele illustrates the coquette (Mrs. Toss) with concrete mannerisms and hypocrisies. When assessing female character-types in this period or in imitation, check for performative, contradictory behaviors intended to attract social advantage (affectation, selective attention, feigned modesty) and for how these behaviors undermine 'natural' charms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Critic and Wit
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic is described as silliest of mortals, inuring himself to examine all things for passing sentence, relying on authorities, and thus never a companion but always a censor; the wit lacks judgment, is carried away by imagination, invents occasions for his sallies, and often contrives rather than responds to the moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steele gives behavioral standards to judge these roles: critics over-apply judgment, lean on precedent/authority, and become pedantic; wits should ideally produce remarks arising naturally from time and place rather than manufactured novelty. Use these traits as evaluative dimensions when judging persons, characters, or rhetorical styles in essays: sincerity of occasion, reliance on authority, social usefulness, and whether wit/criticism serves conversation or self-display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice for Early Love-Poets / Practice Before Ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: It is ordinary for love to make men poetical; before attempting grand works (an heroic poem) a man should try his vein on the lady's confidantes or retinue — smaller, safer audiences — rather than make an heroic poem his first attempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is prescriptive guidance about craft and audience: cultivate skill and test verse on more attainable circles before ambitious publication. The page illustrates with the anecdote of a suitor flattering a parrot and composing modest verses. When evaluating novice poets (historical or modern analogues), value graduated practice and attention to audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtship Strategy: Imitation vs Possession (parrot/dove metaphor)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be loved, a man must imitate the parrot (constant flattering display); the dove represents possession of the beloved — parrot-like behavior wins the courtship, dove-like behavior preserves the conquest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rhetorical metaphor functions as practical criterion in assessing courtship conduct in the essays: successful pursuit often requires active, visible flattery rather than silent possession. Use this when interpreting characters' romantic tactics or satiric points about gender relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social Labels and Offence ('smart fellow' test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Calling a gentleman a 'smart fellow' is an appellation of praise and not an affront; it becomes offensive only if the accused denies the description (i.e., if someone says he is not a 'smart fellow'). A 'smart fellow' is identified by vivacity, a jerking motion, well-fancied lining of coat — outward vivacity/dress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steele offers a social-pragmatic test for insult vs compliment: context and self-identification matter. When assessing social interactions or satirical dialogue, consider whether a term is taken as praise by local fashion codes and whether injury is caused by contestation of the label rather than its use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custom as Explanation for Irrational Social Practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Custom — the force of fashion, dress, and chivalry encouraged by ladies — explains why even men of sense, virtue, and experience comply with practices like duelling; they conform to avoid ridicule and to appear agreeable to mistresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a sociological criterion: when explaining apparently irrational behavior, prioritize the role of custom, conformity, and desire for social acceptance rather than purely individual reason. Use this explanatory principle in literary-historical readings of conduct and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duelling as an Illegitimate Offshoot of Knight-Errantry / National Modes of Honour
rubrics_metrics.description: The duel is taken to be an illegitimate species of ancient knight-errantry: modern single combats are chimerical monsters created after the extinction of 'real' monsters (dragons). National manners differ — e.g., Spaniards stab in revenge, Englishmen challenge fairly — and some societies limit the bearing of arms to mercenaries or professions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steele frames duelling historically and comparatively: evaluate duelling by its genealogy (chivalric imitation) and by national customs. When analyzing representations of honor, note whether violence is ritualized, socially regulated, or symptomatic of fashion-driven affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-hand Vice and Imitation as Particularly Reprehensible
rubrics_metrics.description: Second-hand vice — imitators and mimics of rakes and fashions — is described as the most nauseous form of vice; imitators spread affectation and cause honest people to misbehave to avoid ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supplies an ethical-evaluative yardstick: originality of vice (one's own vice) is less contemptible than the social contagion of affectation. Use this when judging characters' moral responsibility and the social impact of fashionable behavior in satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fashion & Social Classification by Accoutrements and Habits (e.g., snuff, dress)
rubrics_metrics.description: Social rank and type are signalled by possessions and habits (e.g., the shape of a snuff-box, whether one takes Spanish or musty snuff, the cut and lining of a coat). Carter/merchant names (Charles Mather, Charles Lillie) and captured 'musty' snuff are cited as cultural particulars propagating fashion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material culture functions as evidence for social classification in Steele's prose: when annotating or reconstructing social worlds, attend to small consumer details, tobacconist references, and taste-signals as criteria for placing a person within town society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical Measure of 'Honour' and Military Display
rubrics_metrics.description: Public measures of honour and martial reputation are satirized: civic militia and mercenary spectacle transform bravery into display and commodity (one may 'measure a man's services by his waist'); public battles are represented theatrically to give people sight of their 'money's' advantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this standard when interpreting Steele's ironies about honour: evaluate claims to bravery by whether they are spectacle/commodity rather than substantive courage. Look for satiric inversion (wealth enabling rank; public representation supplanting real service) as a recurring criterion for criticism.
